content: Blurred vision is a frequent ocular symptom characterized by either a sudden or gradual reduction in the clarity or sharpness of vision, making it difficult to perceive fine details. It can affect one eye (unilateral) or both eyes (bilateral). There is limited historical information available regarding the origins or historical understanding of blurred vision. Currently, there is no standardized system for classifying blurred vision. The underlying mechanisms of blurred vision can involve refractive errors, opacities in ocular structures such as the lens, cornea, or vitreous, retinal disorders, or diseases affecting the optic nerve. Blurred vision can arise from a variety of conditions, including: Refractive errors (the most common cause) Age-related macular degeneration Cataracts Presbyopia Diabetic retinopathy Glaucoma Corneal abrasions, scarring, or keratitis Conjunctivitis Uveitis or iritis Retinal detachment Retinitis Ocular trauma, such as hyphema Migraines Malignancies or tumors (e.g., brain tumors, metastatic lung cancer, leukemia) Optic neuritis Cerebrovascular diseases, such as transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) or strokes Vasculitis, including temporal arteritis or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Hypertension Side effects of medications Blurred vision can affect individuals of all ages. By the age of 65, approximately one in three people will have some form of vision-reducing eye disorder. Screening recommendations include: The American Diabetes Association advises that individuals with type 1 diabetes undergo a comprehensive eye examination within five years of diagnosis, while those with type 2 diabetes should have an eye exam at the time of diagnosis. Annual follow-ups are recommended thereafter. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine glaucoma screening, but the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) suggests that individuals at higher risk, such as African Americans and older adults, consult their healthcare provider for advice. The prognosis for blurred vision depends on the underlying cause. Complications and outcomes vary widely based on the specific condition responsible for the symptom. There are no universally established diagnostic criteria for blurred vision. Diagnosis relies on a detailed medical history and a thorough eye examination. Patients should be asked about the onset, duration, associated symptoms, and whether the blurred vision affects one or both eyes. Common symptoms accompanying blurred vision include eye redness, pain, excessive tearing (epiphora), headaches, light sensitivity (photophobia), halos around lights, nausea, excessive thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), dizziness, and numbness. Physical examination for blurred vision includes: Visual acuity testing Visual field assessment Slit-lamp examination Ophthalmoscopy Tonometry Gonioscopy (angle testing) The presence of sudden hemiplegia, abnormal gait, ataxia, or dysarthria may indicate a cerebrovascular accident. Laboratory tests may be necessary for systemic conditions: Elevated blood sugar and hemoglobin A1C levels are seen in diabetic patients with blurred vision. Urinalysis and renal function tests are recommended for patients with hypertension. Antinuclear antibodies and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are associated with SLE and vasculitis. A complete blood count (CBC) with differential and other tests may be required in cases of leukemia or multiple myeloma. Imaging studies may assist in diagnosis: A CT scan of the brain can help identify mass lesions, ischemic strokes, or hemorrhagic strokes. MRI of the brain and orbits can confirm optic nerve inflammation. Treatment for blurred vision depends on the underlying cause: Refractive errors and presbyopia are managed with corrective lenses or eyeglasses. Supportive care for hyphema includes elevating the head of the bed, wearing an eye shield, and reducing physical activity. Dry macular degeneration has no specific treatment, but wet macular degeneration can be managed with anti-VEGF medications or photodynamic therapy to inhibit abnormal blood vessel growth. Medical therapies include: Intravitreal injections of anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenesis agents (e.g., anti-VEGF drugs) for diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema. Laser therapy for diabetic retinopathy. Eye drops for glaucoma management. Antibacterial, antiviral, or antiparasitic agents for infectious causes. Corticosteroids for uveitis, iritis, and optic neuritis. High-dose corticosteroids for temporal arteritis. Antihypertensive medications for hypertension. Surgical interventions include: LASIK for refractive errors. Cataract surgery and retinal detachment repair. Vitrectomy for diabetic retinopathy. Glaucoma surgeries such as trabeculoplasty, iridotomy, and trabeculectomy. Primary prevention strategies include maintaining a healthy lifestyle, controlling hypertension, managing lipid levels, and undergoing regular eye examinations. Smoking cessation is particularly important to reduce the risk of age-related macular degeneration. These interventions include weight management, antihypertensive therapy, statin use, antiplatelet therapy, diabetes management, and smoking cessation.
